ablation: by removing each major component one at a time (leave everything else identical) to measure its standalone contribution to the metric
by replacing each major component with a minimal baseline version (simplest reasonable alternative) to test whether complexity is actually earning metric gains
by ablating each input signal/source independently (drop one source/feature group at a time) to quantify which inputs drive performance
by running 'only-X' variants (keep only one source/feature group while dropping the rest) to reveal which inputs are sufficient on their own
by disabling each preprocessing/normalization/augmentation step individually to see which data handling steps are beneficial vs. incidental
by removing each constraint/regularizer/penalty term (or its equivalent) individually to test whether it improves generalization vs. just changes optimization behavior
by turning off each post-processing step (thresholding, smoothing, rule filters, calibration, reranking, etc.) to see whether gains come from the core method or downstream tweaks
by substituting any learned/scored decision rule with a simple fixed rule (e.g., default threshold, uniform weighting, uncalibrated score) to isolate the value of the learned decision logic
by testing an 'identity' ablation for each transformation stage (skip the transform so inputs flow through unchanged) to confirm the transform is doing useful work
by reducing capacity/expressiveness wherever applicable (fewer parameters, fewer layers/steps, smaller embedding/dimension, fewer rules/experts) to assess whether performance depends on scale
by increasing capacity/expressiveness wherever applicable (more parameters, more layers/steps, larger dimension, more rules/experts) to check if performance is bottlenecked by under-capacity
by ablating any iterative/refinement stage (run a single pass instead of multiple passes) to measure the value of refinement versus the base pass
by ablating any stochastic element (disable randomness, sampling, dropout-like behavior, or exploration) to see whether randomness helps the metric or just adds variance
by swapping any domain-specific heuristic with a domain-agnostic default (generic heuristic / no heuristic) to test whether gains rely on handcrafted knowledge
by removing any external dependency (retrieval, tools, caches, auxiliary models, external resources) to quantify how much metric performance comes from external information versus the method itself
